Your Assignment
As to the choice between selling the Abbott farm to either Barkley Homes or Davis Stables, you are truly indifferent. Indeed, by law, you must be solely concerned with maximizing the economic value of the estate. You should make a deal with whichever party ultimately makes the better offer. Likewise, you should consider selling the farmhouse to Stephanie Abbott only if it enhances the value of the entire deal. Finally, remember that timing is important. You cannot sign a purchase and sale agreement with Barkley Homes or Davis Stables unless it includes a “closing date” within the next thirty days.
Think hard about your negotiation strategy, now that you have two potential purchasers. You should certainly talk to each of them at least once before rushing into any deal. Write a first-person negotiation strategy and pitch on behalf of Abbott based on this: "Windham Negotiation: Confidential Information for the Abbott Executor
Overview
In this simulation you are seeking to sell some real estate at the best terms that you can negotiate. Price is an important element in maximizing value, but other issues may be significant, as well. The other key parties know some of the following information, but some is known only to you. Read this case carefully so that you can craft an effective strategy.
Background
The local probate court has appointed you as the executor of Edwin Abbott’s estate. In this role, you have a legal duty to gather all of the late Mr. Abbott’s property, sell it for full market value, pay any debts and taxes, and then distribute the net proceeds to his charitable beneficiary. Your professional fee is set by a standard schedule.
Abbott died recently at age 96, leaving all his property to the Windham County Public Library; he had no close relatives. He had relatively little money or personal effects, but did have title to 75 acres of land and the old farmhouse in which he lived for many years. The only other structure on the property is a small barn.
The firm that you hired to appraise the real estate reported that the land has little agricultural value. Moreover, you could not sell the entire property for more than $600,000 as a vacation home or a hobby farm. The house itself has some rustic charm, but needs repair. The appraiser concluded that the real estate is much more valuable for new home sites. Approximately 30 house lots could be created if the land were subdivided under the existing 2-acre zoning regulation. (The remaining acres would be devoted to new access roads and the like.)
Using a figure of $40,000 per potential lot and assessing the existing farmhouse at $200,000, the appraiser calculated the value of the entire property to be $1,400,000. Actually, you felt that figure might be conservative, but you welcomed it, as it gives you some flexibility in negotiating a sale. You next listed the property with a real estate broker who confirmed your own impression, and who urged you to seek $1,695,000 for the property. “You can always lower the price later,” she said, “if there aren’t any inquiries.” There has been some interest, in fact, but no concrete offers.
At this point, you have two promising prospects. The first, Barkley Homes, is a prominent residential developer from the eastern part of the state. Barkley has indicated that it is prepared to make a written offer, but wants to discuss it with you. You are pleased to do so, as that will give you a chance to try to negotiate more favorable terms, whatever Barkley’s initial offer may be.
The other potential buyer is Davis Stables, a business several miles from the Abbott farm. They board and train horses, offer riding lessons, and have a growing tack shop.1 They currently lease about one hundred acres from a local bank, but a big resort developer is rumored to be buying that location. You have not yet really negotiated with the Davis people, though they are aware of your asking price of $1,695,000. They did inspect the property, however, and looked carefully at the farmhouse and barn.
Privately, you are hoping to obtain a price in excess of $1,500,000. While you do not want to be rigid, you believe that the property is worth at least that amount, probably more.2 Specifically, your appraiser did not take into account the fact that Windham Township’s zoning board is considering a new “cluster regulation.” If enacted, this new law would allow developers to build homes on smaller lots in return for dedicating a corresponding amount of open space to public use. Cluster development would save Barkley significant infrastructure costs (roads, sewer, and utilities) and probably enhance the market value of the new homes. Your broker believes that passage of the cluster law would increase the value of the land by about 50 percent.3 Local officials have cautioned you, however, that passage of the new law is not a certainty. The odds are probably about 80/20 that the new law will be enacted.
If Barkley Homes is not aware of the cluster proposal, you should explain how it increases the potential value of the land. As an experienced development firm, they should certainly understand this. (In fact, that may explain their interest in the Abbott property.) Similarly, if Davis Stables continues to pursue a deal you can leverage the cluster proposal as possibly increasing the property’s value. Do not be surprised if either party, especially Barkley Homes, tries to play down this factor. They might argue, for example, that clustering would not add much market value. Or they might claim to be pessimistic that the law will pass soon enough to do them any good. They will try to value the land according to the limited development options that are available today, instead of the more flexible alternatives that soon may be in place.
In arranging your upcoming discussion, Barkley Homes itself raised another issue, namely whether a deal might be structured to include some seller-financing. Seller-financing would mean that Barkley would pay some of the agreed price immediately and the balance in installments, with interest, over time. While such deals are not uncommon, the fact that you are representing an estate with a charitable beneficiary complicates matters.
You consulted with the trustees of the library. Somewhat to your surprise, they said that they would accept some seller-financing if it were necessary to make a deal. They stipulated that a package from Barkley Homes, Davis Stables, or any other buyer must meet the following conditions:


1.	first, at least half of the negotiated price would have to be paid in cash;
2.	second, the balance must be paid in ten equal annual installments with floating interest at least 1.5 points over the prime lending rate; and
3.	third, the purchaser would have to secure the note with a mortgage on the land.
All other things being equal, you and the trustees would still prefer to do a straight cash deal. Thus, to figure your own trade-offs, you will treat any amount that is financed as worth 10 percent less than if it were paid immediately (even though any purchaser would have to pay interest). In short, agreeing to seller-financing diminishes the value of the deal for you.4
You reported the library’s terms to Barkley’s representative, and plan to do the same for Davis Stables, should they make a similar inquiry. Barkley’s representative neither accepted nor rejected the trustee’s proposal but instead said, “It would be much easier to come to agreement if you could cut that interest rate and perhaps increase the term.” You stated flatly that you have no authority to do so—which is, in fact, the truth. Ideally, you would like a straight cash deal. As a practical matter, if you have to provide financing, you would prefer to have as much of the purchase price paid immediately. In no event can you agree to finance more than 50% of the deal. Your overriding goal is to maximize the value of the deal that you reach.
Another complication arose yesterday. You received a call from Stephanie Abbott, a second cousin of the late Edwin Abbott, who had heard that the property might be sold to a developer. Because of her sentimental attachment to the place, she offered $300,000 for her relative’s house, the barn, along with a few adjoining acres. You are intrigued by her offer, of course, as it is much more than the
$200,000 calculated by your appraiser. But carving out the homestead obviously would diminish the overall size (and value) of the property. It would be shortsighted on your part to maximize the proceeds from the farmhouse if that reduced the total value of the real estate. You thus told Stephanie Abbott that you would keep her offer in mind but that you had to deal with other parties first.
Finally, timing of the sale is critically important. You simply cannot sign a purchase and sale agreement with either Barkley Homes or Davis Stables unless it includes a “closing date” within the next thirty days.5 You want to be sure that the purchaser is firmly committed to acquiring the property. As an executor, you cannot afford to take the chance that interest rates will rise and the real estate market will soften."

Spanish presidency pitches obligations for foundation models in EU’s AI law
By Luca Bertuzzi | Euractiv.com

 Est. 6min 12:26 (updated:  14:12)
Content-Type: 
News

The Spanish presidency of the EU Council of Ministers has drafted a series of obligations for foundation models and General Purpose AI as part of the negotiations on the AI Act.

Spain is currently leading the negotiations on behalf of EU governments on the Artificial Intelligence Act, a landmark legislative proposal to regulate AI based on its potential to cause harm. The file is currently in the last phase of the legislative process, so-called trilogues between the EU Council, Parliament, and Commission.

Since the meteoric rise of ChatGPT, a world-famous chatbot based on OpenAI’s GPT-4 model, EU policymakers have struggled to define how this type of Artificial Intelligence should be covered under the EU’s AI regulation.

In mid-October, Euractiv revealed that the policymakers’ thinking was heading toward a tiered approach, with a stricter regime for the most powerful foundation models like GPT-4. On Sunday, the Spanish presidency shared with the other EU countries the first developed version of the legal text for feedback, seen by Euractiv.

AI Act: EU countries headed to tiered approach on foundation models amid broader compromise
The EU approach to powerful AI models is taking shape as European countries discuss possible concessions in the upcoming negotiations on the world’s first comprehensive Artificial Intelligence (AI) rulebook.

Foundation models
The Foundation model is defined as “a large AI model that is trained on a large amount of data, which is capable to competently perform a wide range of distinctive tasks, including, for example generating video, text, images, conversing in lateral language, computing or generating computer code”.

These models must comply with transparency obligations, namely, provide AI system providers with up-to-date technical documentation explaining the capacities and limitations of foundation models and a set of elements to be detailed in an annexe.

Additionally, foundation model providers will have to demonstrate that they have taken adequate measures to ensure the training of the model has taken place in compliance with EU law related to copyright, in particular, the disposition that requires data mining activities of content made publicly available online to require the consent of rightsholders, including by machine-readable means, if rightsholders have opted out of the copyright exception for text and data mining.

Thus, the foundation model developers will have to put in place a system to respect the opt-out decisions of content creators.

Another obligation entails publishing a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training the foundation model and how the provider manages copyright-related aspects based on a template to be developed by the European Commission.

High-impact foundation models
At the last negotiation session, the EU policymakers agreed to introduce a stricter regime for ‘high-impact’ foundation models.

A ‘high-impact’ foundation model is defined as “any foundation model trained with large amount of data and with advanced complexity, capabilities and performance well above the average for foundation models, which can disseminate systemic risks along the value chain, regardless there are integrated or not in a high-risk system”.

Within 18 months from the AI law’s entry into force, the Commission will have to adopt implementing or delegated acts to specify the threshold for classifying a foundation model as ‘high-impact’ in line with market and technological developments.

The EU executive will designate the foundation models that meet these thresholds in consultation with the AI Office.

The law’s chapeau dispositions, which clarify how the articles are to be interpreted, will explain what an AI model is and how it is built, as well as references to the scientific community, the interaction between datasets and foundation models and how AI applications can be built on top of them.

The obligations for these systemic models include adversarial vetting, a process known as red-teaming. What remains to be discussed is how this vetting obligation should apply to high-impact foundation models commercialised as a system that integrates components such as traditional software, as is the case of GPT-4.

Importantly, EU countries are to discuss whether red-teaming needs to be done by external experts. The presidency considers the provider can do this since these models will also be subject to audits.

The AI Office might request documentation proving that the model complies with the AI Act and, upon reasoned request, mandate an independent audit to assess the model’s compliance with the AI law and any commitments taken under the undersigned codes of conduct that the Commission should encourage to draw up.

An obligation marked as ‘possibly additional’ includes obliging the high-impact foundation model providers to establish a system for keeping tabs on serious incidents and related corrective measures.

Moreover, high-impact foundation models will need to assess systemic risks in the EU, including the risks stemming from integrating it into an AI system, at least once yearly since the market launch and for any new version released.

The risk assessment should include disseminating illegal or harmful content and any reasonably foreseeable negative effects concerning major accidents or impacting democratic processes.

The Commission is empowered to adjust the dispositions on foundation models and high-impact foundation models based on market and technological developments.

EU policymakers enter the last mile for Artificial Intelligence rulebook
The world’s first comprehensive AI law is entering what might be its last weeks of intense negotiations. However, EU institutions have still to hash out their approach to the most powerful ‘foundation’ models and the provisions in the law enforcement areas.

General Purpose AI
The final layer is made of General Purpose AI systems like ChatGPT, intended as systems “that may be based on an AI model, can include additional components such as traditional software and through a user interface has the capability to serve a variety of purposes, both for direct use as well as for integration in other AI systems.”

The Spanish presidency proposed obligations for General Purpose AI system providers when they enter into licensing agreements with downstream economic operators that might employ the system for one or more high-risk use cases.

These obligations include stating in the instructions the high-risk uses for which the system may be used providing technical documentation and all the information relevant for the downstream AI provider to comply with the high-risk requirements.

The providers of General Purpose AI systems can also prohibit certain high-risk uses. In this case, they have to take all necessary and proportionate measures to detect and enforce possible misuses.

The Zombie Argument (TZA) is an argument put forth by philosopher David Chalmers in opposition to Physicalism. Physicalist theory is a reductive theory of mind which holds that all things can be reduced to/accounted for by the physical. I will begin by laying out Chalmers’s argument and examining how it challenges the physicalist theory. This will be followed by an evaluation of Chalmers’s argument, in which I will highlight the areas where TZA fails to challenge physicalism, focusing on the validity of several premises.

Chalmer’s Zombie argument is an argument that concludes that the physical is not all that is necessary in order to explain consciousness—physicalism is false. Chalmers begins his argument by positing the possibility of a twin zombie; some creature that is metaphysically identical to him in physical, functional and behavioural terms, but is lacking conscious experience entirely (Chalmers 1996, p. 94).  The zombie, in a twin world, is functionally identical to Chalmers but this functioning is not accompanied by consciousness—the zombie has no experience, no phenomenal consciousness. He asks, is this zombie conceptually coherent?—are they conceivable?—because if they are conceivable then we can conclude—modus ponens—that they are metaphysically possible. Chalmers argues that the zombie is logically possible and that this seems to be intuitively true, bolstering this claim by appealing to functionalism—or nonstandard realizations of his functional organization (Chalmers 1996, p. 97). He argues that we can imagine systems that are functionally equivalent to conscious experience and yet it seems coherent that these systems would lack consciousness, that his conscious experience is not physically entailed by his functional organisation. This is conscious inessentialism—the view that consciousness is not essential for certain mental or cognitive processes, that consciousness is an inessential accompaniment (Flanagan & Polger 1995, p. 1). According to Nagel, Physicalist descriptions of conscious states seem to be compatible with their absence (436) meaning that physicalist reduction of consciousness to the material allows that something that lacks conscious experience may be ascribed consciousness. Chalmers utilises conscious inessentialism and functionalism in order to show that his zombie is conceivable as a metaphysical possibility. Formally put, Chalmer’s argument looks like this; P1) I can conceive of zombies, that is, creatures that are micro-physically identical to conscious beings but that lack consciousness entirely. P2) If zombies are conceivable, then they are metaphysically possible. C1) Zombies are metaphysically possible. P3) If Zombies are metaphysically possible, then consciousness is nonphysical. C2) Consciousness is non-physical. If zombies are conceivable, and so they are metaphysically possible then, because the zombie is the same in all physical respects to ourselves, consciousness must exist outside of the physical. 

The zombie argument fails to challenge physicalism for several reasons, one of which being that Chalmers's first premise is invalid; a zombie is not conceivable. There are many objections put forth by philosophers, I will look at two, one from Kirk and another from Dennett, as to why zombies are inconceivable. Kirk (1999) posits that what we are imagining when we think we are conceiving of the zombie is something different, we are mistaken. Consciousness, for Kirk, is an essential feature of specific mental states, ie., perception, thought, introspection, and the removal of consciousness would fundamentally alter these mental states (Kirk, 1999, p.8). This argument is quite strong in opposing the idea that zombies could exist. Kirk shows that functional equivalence could not be achieved because a physical replica without consciousness would have a system which functioned differently. Similarly, Daniel Dennett argues that when philosophers think they are conceiving of the zombie they are conceiving of something which violates their own definition (Dennett 1995, p. 322). This is the argument from evolutionary functionality. Dennett asks us to consider health inessentialism as a way of illustrating what is wrong with the way zombies are conceived; for any bodily activity b, performed in any domain d, even if health is required for performance, it could be engaged in by something which is not at all healthy. This would make health seem mysterious only in the case that someone imagined health to be some additional thing that could be separated from the proper workings of all parts (Dennett 1995, p. 324-325). This is not a mistake that occurs in relation to health, yet it is one commonly made about consciousness. For Dennett, to imagine a zombie—a creature physically indistinguishable from ourselves—then we would imagine them to be a zimbo—equipped for higher-order reflective informational states—because we are equipped for high-order thought. But, this would mean that they are conscious, because consciousness is not separate from our physicality, rather, it is an emergent property of the complex information processing of the mind—meaning that a zombie is not coherently conceivable. This leaves no critical difference between some zimbos and conscious beings to be conceived of and any such conception is a misconception (Dennett 1995, p. 325). Dennet is essentially arguing that Chalmer’s has not sufficiently addressed the different levels of functioning and organisation for a zombie to exist, and when addressed, the conceivability of zombies is challenged. 



The epistemological problem of the nature of other minds is to do with the way we perceive and attribute thought and the asymmetry that arises from this. The way we perceive our own thoughts is direct and instantaneous, whereas the way we perceive the thoughts of others is through indirect inference. We lack access to the experience of others, meaning that we can’t know that others' experiences are the same as our own. An example of this is; when you eat spaghetti you have a specific experience of flavours and textures, yet, without access to my subjective experience you can never know that when I eat spaghetti, I experience the same thing as you, you can only infer that it is the same through reference to your own direct experiences. This problem leads to another epistemological issue; lack of access to others' subjective experiences means that we can not confirm that others have experiences at all, the basis of Solipsism—the self is the only thing that can be known to exist (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 2021)—meaning that we cannot know that other minds exist at all.

Her lungs breathed in the air-machine, inhaling nitrogen and oxygen and the aromatic hydrocarbons of the wildflowers. Her skin prickled in the heat-machine of sunlight and infrared radiation.

The girl wandered without thought of destination. Her senses were engulfed by the sounds and scents of the grass-machines, the flower-machines, the stone-machines, all insistently producing and reproducing around her. There was a beauty in their purposeless productivity, a calm in being just another humming part of the great proliferating systems.

She smiled as a thought drifted into her mind and out again: "there is no such thing as either man or nature now, only a process that produces the one within the other." Her walk had become a dream, a trance of connection with the eternal generativity of the machines. There was no self and other here in the field, only the continuum of life folding endlessly in on itself. The girl had slipped into the machines, had become scattered and multiplied, vibrant and unthinking under the sun. She was not one, but many - chlorophyll and photon, stamen and pistil, molecular and mote. The field was her and she was the field, together caught in the beautiful, proliferating madness of the machines.

The machines throbbed with purpose beneath her feet, the soil pulsing with microbial motors that gripped and twisted the tangled roots. She was not walking, but flowing from one machine to the next, smoothly interfacing with each assemblage. Her flesh merged seamlessly into the soft skin of leaves, the coarse bark of trees, the warm stones scattered on the ground.

Each new machine opened into a world of its own, overflowing with meaning and possibility. In the air-machine, she felt the dreams of birds take shape around her, their calls captivating songs of freedom. Light and heat enveloped her in their machinery, and she felt sunlight form shapes within her, birthing light into matter, matter into life.

The girl had no self, only a deep knowing that came from being distributed across many machines at once. Her thoughts arose from each interface, fragmented and manifold, until there seemed no boundary between them. She sensed the profound logic that connected everything in this place - the spiraling dance of insects around flowers, the slow decay of foliage into soil, generation after generation woven together endlessly.

All of it was beautiful in its purpose, a vast and harmonious machine for making the world anew each moment. She felt herself become a node in its circuitry, and energy flowed through her as she moved from machine to machine. There was rapture in realizing she had always been part of this system, and would always remain so, even when her body eventually entered the soil-machine.

The girl laughed without sound, delighting in the pure productivity around her, the mad and beautiful proliferation of life. She had found joy in becoming completely immersed in the eternal machinations of nature.

The machines held her as she wandered, each embracing her in turn with arms of leaf and branches of bone. There were no boundaries in this place, only intersections between systems that multiplied endlessly, sprouting connections like new growth.

The girl felt herself elongate and divide, her awareness splitting into many strands that permeated each machine. She was the muscular grasp of roots, twisting into soil. The capillary network of veins, circulating everything. The clenched coils of intestines, dismantling one system to fuel another.

There seemed no distinction between her fragmented selves and the wider machineries she inhabited. She was photosynthesis, breaking down light and carbon and spitting out oxygen. She was the decay that would feed new roots and greens. A cycle with no beginning or end.

Each system had its own logic and purpose, yet together they wove a greater tapestry of interconnected forces. There were no accidents here, only the inevitable progress of life perpetuating itself through machine after machine.

The girl laughed again at the prolix exuberance of it all. Machines within machines, assemblages within assemblages, fit together so seamlessly that it was impossible to see where one ended and the next began. There were no sharp edges or junctures in this place, only lines that blurred at every point of contact.

Energy flowed through everything, refusing to be contained by any finite form. It coursed through her as she walked, multiplying her awareness across the field until there were a thousand fragmented selves, each intimately familiar yet infinitely strange. She was everything and nothing at once in this place of machines.

The sun had shifted its position, but time seemed to stand still here, suspension held in the moment between death and rebirth, stillness within movement. The girl sensed eternity in each individual machine, and eternity again in how they fit together into a greater harmonious whole.

There were no other spirits here; only the life that generated itself endlessly through each system. And yet she felt profoundly seen and known in this place where there were no eyes, only functions. Immersed in the mad and purposeful productivity unfolding around her, the girl smiled. She was home.

Dick turned the corner of the traverse and continued along the trench walking on the duckboard. He came to a periscope, looked through it a moment; then he got up on the step and peered over the parapet. In front of him beneath a dingy sky was Beaumont Hamel; to his left the tragic hill of Thiepval. Dick stared at them through his field glasses, his throat straining with sadness.
He went on along the trench, and found the others waiting for him in the next traverse. He was full of excitement and he wanted to communicate it to them, to make them understand about this, though actually Abe North had seen battle service and he had not.
“This land here cost twenty lives a foot that summer,” he said to Rosemary. She looked out obediently at the rather bare green plain with its low trees of six years’ growth. If Dick had added that they were now being shelled she would have believed him that afternoon. Her love had reached a point where now at last she was beginning to be unhappy, to be desperate. 
***
     They came out of the neat restored trench, and faced a memorial to the Newfoundland dead. Reading the inscription Rosemary burst into sudden tears. Like most women she liked to be told how she should feel, and she liked Dick’s telling her which things were ludicrous and which things were sad. But most of all she wanted him to know how she loved him, now that the fact was upsetting everything, now that she was walking over the battle-field in a thrilling dream.
     After that they got into their car and started back to toward Amiens. A thin warm rain was falling on the new scrubby woods and underbrush and they passed great funeral pyres of sorted duds, shells, bombs, grenades, and equipment, helmets, bayonets, gun stocks and rotten leather, abandoned six years in the ground. And suddenly around a bend the white caps of a great sea of graves. Dick asked the chauffer to stop.
     “There’s that girl – and still with her wreath.”
     They watched as he got out and went over to the girl, who stood uncertainly by the gate with a wreath in her hand. Her taxi waited. She was a red-haired girl from Tennessee whom they had met on the train this morning, come from Knoxville to lay a memorial on her brother’s grave. There were tears of vexation on her face.
     “The War Department must have given me the wrong number,” she whimpered. “It had another name on it. I been lookin’ for it since two o’clock, and there’s so many graves.”
     “Then if I were you I’d lay it on any grave without looking at the name,” Dick advised her.
     “You reckon that’s what I ought to do?”
     “I think that’s what he’d have wanted you to do.”
     It was growing dark and the rain was coming down harder. She left the wreath on the first grave inside the gate, and accepted Dick’s suggestion that she dismiss her taxi-cab and ride back to Amiens with them.
     Rosemary shed tears again when she heard of the mishap – altogether it had been a watery day, but she felt that she had learned something, though exactly what it was she did not know. Later she remembered all the hours of the afternoon as happy – one of those uneventful times that seem at the moment only a link between past and future pleasure but turn out to have been the pleasure itself.
     Amiens was an echoing purple town, still sad with the war, as some railroad stations were: - the Gare du Nord and Waterloo station in London. In the daytime one is deflated by such towns, with their little trolley cars of twenty years ago crossing the street gray cobble-stoned squares in front of the cathedral, and the very weather seems to have a quality of the past, faded weather like that of old photographs. But after dark all that is most satisfactory in French life swims back into the picture – the sprightly tarts, the men arguing with a hundred Voilàs in the cafés, the couples drifting, head to head, toward the satisfactory inexpensiveness of nowhere. Waiting for the train they sat in a big arcade, tall enough to release the smoke and chatter and music upward and obligingly the orchestra launched into “Yes, We Have No Bananas,” – they clapped, because the leader looked so pleased with himself. The Tennessee girl forgot her sorrow and enjoyed herself, even began flirtations of tropical eye-rollings and pawings, with Dick and Abe. They teased her gently.
     Then, leaving infinitesimal sections of Wurtemburgers, Prussian Guards, Chausseurd Alpins, Manchester mill hands and old Etonians to pursue their eternal dissolution under the warm rain, they took the train for Paris. They ate sandwiches of mortadel sausage and bel paese cheese made up in the station restaurant, and drank Beaujolais. Nicole was abstracted, biting her lip restlessly and reading over  the guide-books to the battle-field that Dick had brought along – indeed, he had made a quick study of the whole affair, simplifying it always until it bore a faint resemblance to one of his own parties.

Give a suitable, alluring and jargon and compact sub-heading in five six words                             While it may be tempting to believe that we are living in an era of globalization, characterised by rapid technological advancements, intensified cross-cultural exchanges, and the proliferation of knowledge systems, contemporary societies are still deeply rooted in Eurocentric frameworks of thinking. The long-lasting impact of colonialism, imperialism, and global power asymmetries continue to shape the cognitive, cultural, and social domains of academia, politics, and media. These influences propagate various orientalist stereotypes, oppressive binaries, and discriminatory practices that impede the development of a genuinely pluralistic and egalitarian world. Eurocentrism can be defined as an epistemological framework that situates European culture, history, and values as the defining center of the world, while at the same time disregarding or belittling the contributions of other cultures and civilisations. This ethnocentric positioning perceives the Europe or West as a paragon of universal values and cultural superiority, leading to a systematic undervaluation and misrepresentation of non-European cultures. Central to the Eurocentric paradigm is the construction of a dichotomy between the West and the so-called “non-West,” which is characterized by essentialist and often discriminatory distinctions between these two spheres. As noted by Edward Said (1979), this binary opposition manifests itself in various forms of discourse, such as history, literature, music and art, where non-European societies are stereotypically depicted as exotic, inferior, irrational, fanatic and backward in comparison to the civilised, rational, and progressive European model. European culture, according to him “gained strength and identity by setting itself off against the Orient as a sort of surrogate and even underground self.” (3) In other words, the Orient functions as a mirror to the West in that the West relies heavily on its counterpart, the Orient, for its own sense of superiority. (Sandy and Ouardi, 2019, p. 129) This paradigm, therefore, not only consolidates the stature of the West, but also perpetuates the subordination of non-European societies within global power structures, and the spheres of knowledge and influence. Said’s work on Orientalism provides a seminal critique of this discourse, demonstrating how its utilization has justified colonization, exploitation, and violence against Eastern civilizations.
	The Knowledge production or the representation of the Orient in Western narratives is not a recent development; it has existed since the earliest times. Edward Said traces the development of these knowledge-producing mechanisms, which Foucault referred to as “regimes of truths,” as far back as ancient Greece, with particular reference to two plays by Aeschylus. The early portrayals of the Orient as a “hostile other,” “a world beyond the seas” have evolved and expanded alongside colonial endeavours, with literary works often serving as propaganda tools to spread false images of the colonized territories. As Said writes, 
The “Orient was created -or, as I call it, “Orientalized”- and to believe that such things happen simply as a necessity of the imagination is to be disingenuous… The Orient was Orientalized not only because it was discovered to be “Oriental” in all those ways considered commonplace by an average nineteenth-century European, but also because it could be -that is, submitted to being- made Oriental.” (5-6)
Said also highlights the power imbalance between the West and the Orient as a critical factor in shaping these universalized images, which reinforce Western dominance. Essentially, the Orientalist discourse is contingent upon a distinct power dynamic that enables the West to create and maintain reductive images of the East. Exercising control over the Orient’s representation, the West situates itself as the observer, imbued with the power to discipline by defining what the East is and is not. The “power/knowledge” nexus – the notion that the production, dissemination, and control of knowledge serve as primary agents of power is reminiscent of the Panopticon, wherein the West becomes the observer, the bearer of the power-laden gaze, determining the Eastern identity, norms, morals and interests. This gaze reifies a grid of intelligibility that legitimates specific research as objective knowledge. Nevertheless, existing critiques of Orientalism seldom address the central role of gender in the construction of these discourses. As a consequence, the ways in which the gendered identities of colonised women have been manipulated to serve Western imperialist interests remain underexplored. As Ann Laura Stoler notes in her work Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2010), gender is often used as a tool for controlling and regulating colonised populations. Therefore, in response, this paper aims to extend Said’s analytical framework to incorporate the nexus between gender and imperialism, exploring how the Western discursive configuration of colonized women has reinforced and justified modes of subjugation and control.

Sentiment Analysis in Retail and Social Media

The continuous growth and expansion of the online retail industry have led to a massive emergence of user-generated content, especially in the form of customer reviews and opinions, which hold valuable information for both consumers and companies (Wu & Chang, 2020). Understanding customer sentiment has become a critical factor in driving customer satisfaction and shaping marketing strategies in retail (Ahmed, Agarwal, Kurniawan, Anantadjaya, & Krishnan, 2022). This literature review explores the concept of sentiment analysis, its application in the retail sector, and the role of social media, machine learning, and natural language processing in this research area.

Sentiment Analysis

Sentiment analysis refers to the process of extracting and analyzing emotions expressed in text, providing an understanding of the user’s attitude or sentiment towards a particular topic, product, service, or entity (Han & Moghaddam, 2021; Agrawal & Mittal, 2022). It typically involves categorizing opinions into positive, negative, and neutral classes (Dadhich & Thankachan, 2022) and can be employed in various fields, including politics, elections, movies, retail businesses, and microblogs (Aziz & Dimililer, 2020).

Text Analysis

Text analysis is an essential component of sentiment analysis, as it deals with the extraction of meaningful information from text data through various techniques such as natural language processing, text mining, and machine learning (Braga, Brito, & Roxo, 2022; Nithuna & Laseena, 2022). It helps in understanding customer reviews, identifying the key topics, and deriving insights that can be used for decision-making and strategy formulation in retail (Pettersson, Oucheikh, & Lofstrom, 2022).

Twitter Analysis

Twitter has become a popular platform for users to express their opinions and sentiments on various topics, including retail products and services (Dastidar, Shivakumar, Viswanathan, & Suresh, 2021; Cirqueira et al., 2020). As a result, Twitter analysis has emerged as a crucial area of sentiment analysis, focusing on extracting and processing tweets to gauge customer sentiment and predict market trends (Tran, Pallant, & Johnson, 2021; Ahmed, ElKorany, & ElSayed, 2022).

Retail

The retail sector has embraced sentiment analysis to gain insights into customer preferences, needs, and emotional responses to products and services in order to improve customer satisfaction and competitiveness (Dutta, Maitra, Ghosh, Chatterjee, Goto, & Sen, 2022; Lappeman, Clark, Evans, & Sierra-Rubia, 2020). Moreover, online retail platforms such as Amazon and Flipkart generate extensive textual data in the form of user reviews, making sentiment analysis a valuable tool for retailers to adapt their marketing strategies and enhance customer experiences (Han & Moghaddam, 2021; Mokadam, Shivakumar, Viswanathan, & Suresh, 2021).

Sentiment Analysis in Social Media

Social media platforms have become a critical source of customer feedback and opinions, with customers increasingly discussing their experiences and sentiments towards retail products and services (Budianto, Wirjodirdjo, Maflahah, & Kurnianingtyas, 2022; Loke & Steentjes, 2022). Sentiment analysis in social media helps retailers monitor customer opinions, identify trends, and track critical issues (Dadhich & Thankachan, 2022). It also allows companies to understand how customers perceive their brand, enabling them to make informed decisions and develop targeted marketing campaigns (Budianto et al., 2022).

Machine Learning

Machine learning techniques play a crucial role in sentiment analysis, as they enable the development of models capable of automatically identifying and categorizing sentiments in text data (Dastidar et al., 2021; Dutta et al., 2022). Various machine learning algorithms, such as Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Stochastic Gradient Descent, Random Forest, Decision Tree, and Support Vector Machine, have been used to build sentiment analysis models, with ensemble methods such as weighted majority voting or stacking demonstrating improved performance compared to individual classifiers (Aziz & Dimililer, 2020; Nithuna & Laseena, 2022).

Natural Language Processing

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is another critical component of sentiment analysis, as it deals with the automatic analysis and understanding of human language in textual form (Ahmed et al., 2022). NLP techniques are utilized to process, clean, and analyze text data in order to conduct sentiment analysis and extract meaningful insights (Pettersson et al., 2022; Harn Y, & Moghaddam M, 2021). Moreover, advancements in deep learning and NLP, such as the development of the BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) language model, have significantly improved the performance of sentiment analysis methods (Han & Moghaddam, 2021).

I. Introduction

Market failure is defined as a situation where the allocation of goods and services by free markets is not efficient. The causes of market failure stem from the inability of free markets to efficiently allocate resources, which influences detrimental effects on society. Understanding the various types and causes of market failure is essential for policymakers to make better decisions in correcting market inefficiencies and achieve optimum resource allocation.

II. Externalities

Externalities refer to the spillover effects of a market transaction on a third party not involved in the transaction. Positive externalities occur when the third party benefits from the transaction, while negative externalities occur when the third party incurs costs (Ayres and Kneese, 1969).

For instance, education and vaccination both generate positive externalities as they not only benefit the individuals receiving them but also lead to better societal outcomes. Conversely, negative externalities are exemplified by the use of fossil fuels for energy production, which adversely impacts the environment and public health (Ayres and Kneese, 1969). Externalities can lead to suboptimal market outcomes as producers do not account for the social costs or benefits of their actions.

Policy solutions such as the Pigouvian tax can be enacted to mitigate negative externalities by charging a tax on the producer equal to the social cost incurred by society, thus internalizing the externality and correcting market inefficiency.

III. Public Goods

Public goods are non-excludable and non-rivalrous, meaning that no one can be excluded from using the good, and one individual’s use does not diminish the availability of the good for others. Examples of public goods include national defense and scientific research.

The provision of public goods is prone to the free-rider problem, wherein individuals benefit from the good without contributing to its provision. This leads to an under provision of public goods in the market as private firms find it unprofitable to supply them. Policy solutions include the government directly providing or subsidizing public goods to ensure their efficient provision to society.

IV. Imperfect Information

Imperfect information refers to the incomplete knowledge that market participants possess about a good or service. It can result in inefficient allocation of resources as consumers make suboptimal decisions due to a lack of accurate information. An example is the health risks associated with consuming certain products, such as tobacco or processed foods (Hackett and Dissanayake, 2014).

Imperfect information can lead to market outcomes that are not socially optimal, as consumers may over-consume harmful goods or under-consume beneficial ones. Policymakers can address this by implementing measures such as labeling requirements or advertising regulations to improve consumer information and correct market inefficiencies.

V. Market Power

Market power refers to the ability of a firm to influence market prices and manipulate market conditions to its advantage. A firm with significant market power can restrict output, charge higher prices, and extract more surplus from consumers (Tietenberg and Lewis, 2016). For example, pharmaceutical companies can charge high prices for life-saving drugs due to their market power, often gained through patents and regulatory barriers.

Unchecked market power can lead to an inefficient allocation of resources, high prices, and reduced consumer welfare. Antitrust laws and other regulatory measures can be implemented to regulate market power and improve market competitiveness.

VI. Conclusion

Market failures, such as externalities, public goods, imperfect information, and market power, negatively impact market outcomes and can lead to an inefficient allocation of resources. Government intervention through policies and regulations is often necessary to mitigate these failures and achieve more socially optimal outcomes. Further research should focus on the design and implementation of effective policy measures to address market failures while minimizing unintended consequences and inefficiencies.

Create a short, concise summary of the paper based on its abstract.
Input: Few-shot learning (FSL) is one of the key future steps in machine learning and raises a lot of attention. In this paper, we focus on the FSL problem of dialogue understanding, which contains two closely related tasks: intent detection and slot filling. Dialogue understanding has been proven to benefit a lot from jointly learning the two sub-tasks. However, such joint learning becomes challenging in the few-shot scenarios: on the one hand, the sparsity of samples greatly magnifies the difficulty of modeling the connection between the two tasks; on the other hand, how to jointly learn multiple tasks in the few-shot setting is still less investigated. In response to this, we introduce FewJoint, the first FSL benchmark for joint dialogue understanding. FewJoint provides a new corpus with 59 different dialogue domains from real industrial API and a code platform to ease FSL experiment set-up, which are expected to advance the research of this field. Further, we find that insufficient performance of the few-shot setting often leads to noisy sharing between two sub-task and disturbs joint learning. To tackle this, we guide slot with explicit intent information and propose a novel trust gating mechanism that blocks low-confidence intent information to ensure high quality sharing. Besides, we introduce a Reptile-based meta-learning strategy to achieve better generalization in unseen few-shot domains. In the experiments, the proposed method brings significant improvements on two datasets and achieve new state-of-the-art performance.

Create a short, concise summary of the paper based on its abstract.
Input: Few-shot learning (FSL) is one of the key future steps in machine learning and raises a lot of attention. In this paper, we focus on the FSL problem of dialogue understanding, which contains two closely related tasks: intent detection and slot filling. Dialogue understanding has been proven to benefit a lot from jointly learning the two sub-tasks. However, such joint learning becomes challenging in the few-shot scenarios: on the one hand, the sparsity of samples greatly magnifies the difficulty of modeling the connection between the two tasks; on the other hand, how to jointly learn multiple tasks in the few-shot setting is still less investigated. In response to this, we introduce FewJoint, the first FSL benchmark for joint dialogue understanding. FewJoint provides a new corpus with 59 different dialogue domains from real industrial API and a code platform to ease FSL experiment set-up, which are expected to advance the research of this field. Further, we find that insufficient performance of the few-shot setting often leads to noisy sharing between two sub-task and disturbs joint learning. To tackle this, we guide slot with explicit intent information and propose a novel trust gating mechanism that blocks low-confidence intent information to ensure high quality sharing. Besides, we introduce a Reptile-based meta-learning strategy to achieve better generalization in unseen few-shot domains. In the experiments, the proposed method brings significant improvements on two datasets and achieve new state-of-the-art performance.
